concept: Galaga fidelity — castes, formation, dives, tractor beam, dual fighter, arcade scoring
_why: The director asked for a rebuild closer to the original (components, animation, points, gameplay). This file's predecessor exists because iteration 3 was reported as 'all acceptance gates passed' while half its brief was unbuilt: the requirements were PROSE, so nothing could fail on them. Every requirement here is DATA with a probe name, and tests/star_swarm_galaga_gate_test.php fails when one is missing or when its probe is not asserted inside an expect(...). The probes' strictness is the chair's; the gate checks that none is absent.

sources: https://tips.retrogames.com/gamepage/galaga.html — scoring table, tractor beam, extra ships
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaga — formations, dives, bonus stages, dual fighter
https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Galaga/Gameplay — challenging-stage structure (403 on fetch 2026-09-18; scoring corroborated by the other two)
reference.discrepancy_recorded: Extra-ship thresholds are quoted as 20,000 / 70,000-then-every-70,000 by the GitHub reference and 30,000 / 80,000 by the retrogames page. The DIP default (20,000 then every 70,000) is adopted and asserted as data; the alternative is recorded rather than silently dropped.

observability._why: Behaviour cannot be probed honestly by pixel-guessing alone. The game exposes a minimal read-only surface for tests; it must not become a second code path.

requirements.statement: Three enemy castes exist and are visually distinct, matching Galaga's hierarchy: Bee (yellow/blue), Butterfly (red/white), Boss Galaga (large, four per stage).
requirements.probe: three enemy castes are distinct|bee butterfly and boss
requirements.why: Galaga's structure is the caste system: it drives formation rows, diving behaviour and scoring.

requirements.statement: The player ship and the docked dual fighter are drawn as distinct silhouettes; the dual fighter is visibly two ships.
requirements.probe: dual fighter is two docked ships|dual fighter silhouette
requirements.why: The dual fighter is Galaga's signature power-up and must be recognisable, not a bigger single ship.

requirements.statement: Raster assets stay at zero: every sprite is drawn procedurally (canvas paths), as the current game does.
requirements.probe: no raster assets|procedural sprites
requirements.why: Keeps the module dependency-free and diffable; it is also how a 1981 pixel game is honestly imitated in source.

requirements.statement: The player may have at most two shots in flight at once, as in the arcade original; the limit is observable from the state surface.
requirements.probe: at most two player shots|shot limit
requirements.why: The shot limit is a core difficulty rule, not a detail: it is why Galaga rewards timing.

requirements.statement: Each stage opens with enemies flying in along curved entry paths — from the top and the sides — spinning, then settling into the formation grid.
requirements.probe: entry paths sweep in|formation entry
requirements.why: The entry swoop is the first thing a Galaga player recognises.

requirements.statement: Once assembled the formation breathes — expanding and contracting — rather than being static.
requirements.probe: formation breathes|formation expands and contracts
requirements.why: Galaga's formation visibly pulses; a static grid reads as unfinished.

requirements.statement: Enemies dive out of formation along curved paths, singly, in pairs and in threes, firing as they dive.
requirements.probe: dives singly in pairs and in threes|dive attack
requirements.why: The dive is the attack; formation-only enemies would not be Galaga.

requirements.statement: A destroyed enemy produces an explosion/spin animation, distinct from a plain removal.
requirements.probe: destruction animation|explosion frames
requirements.why: Feedback on the shot is what makes the loop legible.

requirements.statement: Bee scores 50 in formation and 80 in flight (diving).
requirements.probe: bee scores 50 in formation and 80 in flight|bee scoring
requirements.why: Arcade table. In-formation and in-flight values differ for every caste.

requirements.statement: Butterfly scores 80 in formation and 160 in flight.
requirements.probe: butterfly scores 80 in formation and 160 in flight|butterfly scoring
requirements.why: Arcade table.

requirements.statement: Boss Galaga scores 150 in formation, 400 diving alone, 800 with one escort and 1,600 with two escorts.
requirements.probe: boss scores 150 400 800 and 1600|boss escort scoring
requirements.why: Arcade table, including the escort multiplier that makes bosses worth chasing.

requirements.statement: A challenging stage awards 100 per enemy destroyed and a 10,000 perfect bonus for all forty.
requirements.probe: perfect bonus of 10000|challenging stage scoring
requirements.why: The perfect bonus is the single largest score in the original.

requirements.statement: An extra ship is awarded at 20,000 points and every 70,000 after that, and the threshold is observable in state.
requirements.probe: extra ship at 20000|extra ship threshold
requirements.why: Recorded in reference.discrepancy_recorded: the alternative 30,000/80,000 reading exists and is not silently dropped.

requirements.statement: A stage is a cycle — entry, formation, repeated dive waves, stage clear — and difficulty ramps across stages (more enemy projectiles, faster dives).
requirements.probe: difficulty ramps with stage|dive rate increases
requirements.why: Progression is the game; a single static wave is a demo.

requirements.statement: Every fourth stage is a challenging stage where forty enemies fly preset patterns and do not fire.
requirements.probe: every fourth stage is a challenging stage|challenging stage
requirements.why: Stage 3 and every fourth thereafter in the original; it punctuates the loop.

requirements.statement: A Boss Galaga may capture the player's ship with a tractor beam, costing a life; destroying the diving captor frees the ship, which docks as a dual fighter with double firepower and a larger hitbox.
requirements.probe: tractor beam captures the fighter|dual fighter doubles firepower
requirements.why: Galaga's defining mechanic, and the reason the boss exists.

requirements.statement: Destroying the captor while it holds the fighter in formation turns the captured ship into an enemy, rather than freeing it.
requirements.probe: captured fighter turns hostile|hostile captured fighter
requirements.why: The original's sharpest rule and the reason capture is a gamble, not a free upgrade.

requirements.statement: Colliding with an enemy or an enemy shot costs a life; the player respawns with the remaining lives shown in state.
requirements.probe: collision costs a life|lives decrease on hit
requirements.why: The failure condition must be real for the score to mean anything.

requirements.statement: Ships are pixel art, not vector outlines: the game defines bee, butterfly, boss and fighter sprites as in-code pixel matrices (rows of . and #, equal length, at least 8x8), and draws them from that data. No raster assets, so the sprites stay diffable.
requirements.probe: the game exposes sprite pixel matrices|sprite pixel matrices are exposed
requirements.why: The director's finding: gameplay improved while the components looked nothing like Galaga. Vector polygons and anti-aliased curves are the difference the eye names first, and no assertion over state can see it.

requirements.statement: The Boss Galaga is the GREEN magnet ship of the original. Its dominant rendered ink is green-dominant, measured from the sprite's own pixels rather than by name or by a state flag.
requirements.probe: the boss renders green
requirements.why: The boss was orange (--ss-role-threat #f78c6b) while every gate passed, and the boss being green is how the player knows which ship is the magnet ship. Raw colour counts in a formation box are not sufficient: measured 2026-09-19, a box drawn before the colony settled contained bees and reported green for an orange boss. Dominant ink is the fix.

requirements.statement: The play field reads as black space with sparse stars drawn as pixel blocks: at least 90% of the field is near-black once sprites are cleared, and the stars leave no wide band of half-tones.
requirements.probe: the field is black space|stars are pixel blocks
requirements.why: Measured 47% black before the rebuild: a gradient nebula, dust wash and rings replaced the original's empty black, and anti-aliased discs replaced its pixel stars.

requirements.statement: Explosions are hard-edged pixel starbursts with a solid bright core and no soft glow, not anti-aliased stroked rings.
requirements.probe: the burst has a solid core|the explosion is a pixel starburst
requirements.why: A stroked ring is hollow in the middle, which is exactly how the two are told apart. The first version of this probe passed against the very stroked ring it exists to catch.

requirements.statement: The tractor beam is the original's cyan cone: painted cyan, tapering, with horizontal scan lines running down it, and animated rather than static.
requirements.probe: the cone is painted cyan|the tractor beam is a cyan cone
requirements.why: The beam is the magnet ship's signature and the only warning before a capture. The probe stops above the fighter on purpose: the player ship is cyan by role, so a box reaching the bottom would pass on the player's own paint.

requirements.statement: A captured fighter is visibly held by the ship that took it: it is drawn, not merely recorded in state, and it belongs to the capturing ship.
requirements.probe: the captured fighter is drawn under the magnet ship
requirements.why: The capture must be legible as a loss in progress, because shooting the captor is the gamble the original is built around.

requirements.statement: An awarded extra ship at 20,000 and every 70,000 thereafter is ANNOUNCED on screen in the central band of the play field, and the lives count rises by one. Granting it silently is not acceptable.
requirements.probe: extra ship is announced on screen
requirements.why: The director's finding, measured: state.lives rose by one while the rendered band gained exactly zero pixels (before 12, after 12). The mechanic existed and the player could not tell.

requirements.statement: The play field is 16:9 and at least 1280 backing pixels wide, with the formation, player and HUD laid out for the wide field.
requirements.probe: the play field is 16:9
requirements.why: Director decision 2026-09-19: widescreen. The arcade original is portrait (224x288 on a rotated monitor), so this is a deliberate modern reinterpretation, recorded as a deviation rather than presented as fidelity.

requirements.statement: An opening sequence plays BEFORE play begins, on the title screen: it starts on the title stage, advances to a byline stage, and is driven by game time through the update path, exposed as state.opening.stage and readable as state.opening.title and state.opening.byline.
requirements.probe: the game exposes its opening sequence as state|the opening starts on the title
requirements.why: Director request 2026-09-19. Driven by the game clock, not by a wall-clock sleep, so the probe can hold it on a named stage and a red gate stays honest.

requirements.statement: The opening shows 'Star Swarm' as a large pixel-block logo, then 'by IKON' as a smaller pixel-block byline. Both stages carry visible ink in the central band of the field, and the title lockup is markedly the larger mark.
requirements.probe: the title is drawn as logo ink|then the byline is drawn
requirements.why: The order is the requirement: the game's name first, the studio second, both actually rendered rather than present in string state only.

spec_probes._why: Each requirement's probe (or one alias separated by |) must appear inside an expect(...) statement. WHICH spec counts is the anti-faking rule: the behaviour groups (components, animation, points, gameplay) are asserted in tests/browser/star-swarm.spec.ts, and the CHAIR-OWNED groups (fidelity, legibility, opening) are asserted ONLY in tests/browser/star-swarm-pixels.spec.ts, which the rebuild lane must not edit. A lane that can satisfy a requirement by weakening the instrument has proved nothing. Existence is checked mechanically by tests/star_swarm_galaga_gate_test.php; the chair reviews strictness.
spec_probes.rule: existence of the probe name or alias inside expect(...) in the spec that owns the group

invariants._why: No raster assets and no new dependency keep the module diffable. A timing sleep is a race by construction (lesson L4) and is forbidden. The assertion FLOOR (60) is the completed state spec; the BASELINE (52) is what the 52-assertion spec already had, and it is the non-shrink rule applied to a phase. Measured 2026-09-18: a single all-or-nothing gate cannot turn green until the last requirement, so the driver's progress heuristic counted three real chunks (201 lines of product change, gate 12 -> 27) as no progress and escalated. Phases exist so acceptance is satisfiable incrementally; see --phase in tools/harpp2/gates/star_swarm_galaga_gate.php. ADDED 2026-09-19: this contract was satisfied in full while the components did not look like Galaga, because every probe read STATE and none read PIXELS. The state spec says so in its own header. pixel_truth_spec is the answer: rendered-canvas assertions, chair-owned, whose probes the lane cannot edit, and whose floor stops the instrument being shrunk after the fact.
